- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.3) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 1–3% for next period.
- When sentiment is negative (≤0.1) and prices are falling, model often underestimates; adjust upward by 1–2% to avoid missing downward momentum.
- Model frequently overshoots after sharp price spikes (e.g., +5%+ in 3–5 days); apply a “cool-down” rule: cap forecast at 10–15% below peak if sentiment is neutral or slightly negative.
- If sentiment is volatile (alternating 0.1–0.4) and price moves are erratic, reduce forecast horizon smoothing — use 10–15 day moving average instead of 30-day trend.
- When true outcome is significantly below forecast (e.g., >5% gap), check if sentiment was high 3–5 days prior — if yes, apply “sentiment decay” rule: subtract 0.5–1.0% per day of high sentiment.
- If forecast is consistently above true outcome over 3+ consecutive days, apply “mean reversion” correction: subtract 0.5–1.5% per day until price stabilizes or sentiment shifts.
- For long-term (30d) forecasts, if sentiment is low and price is trending down, model often fails to capture the full decline — add a “sentiment-adjusted decay” factor: multiply forecast by (1 - 0.05 * sentiment) if sentiment < 0.2.
